hook: You know “the truth will make you free”. But did you know the sentence begins with an if?
story:
Listen to the answer his hearers give: “We are Abraham’s offspring, and have never been in bondage to anyone.”

Never? Their people’s story begins with slavery in Egypt, where the Egyptians “made their lives bitter with hard service”. And at the very moment they speak, Rome holds their country. Before long their own leaders will say the fear aloud: “the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation”.

It is a very human thing to do, to insist on a freedom one does not fully have.

Jesus does not argue history with them. He goes deeper, to a slavery no army imposes: “everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin”. Then he offers what he came to give: “If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.”
moment:
Jesus is in Jerusalem, in the middle of a long and tense public argument about who he is. Some who are listening want him arrested. Others, John says, have just begun to believe: “As he spoke these things, many believed in him.”

It is to these new believers that he speaks, and he does not flatter them. A moment of belief is not what he is after. He wants them to stay: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples.” The promise of freedom is the second half of that same sentence.
around: The promise hangs on the sentence before it: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples.” When his hearers say they have never been in bondage, he names the bondage he means: “everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin”. He ends: “If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.”
readings:
These words are quoted wherever people praise learning and free inquiry. In that use the truth means knowledge, and knowledge sets a mind free.

Jesus is speaking of something more personal. The truth is what he teaches, and the freedom is freedom from sin. Later in this Gospel he says of himself that he is the truth (John 14:6).

Christians who have lived under oppression have heard a third note in the verse: a freedom no ruler can grant or take away. All three readings honor truth. The second is the one the passage itself gives.
argued:
In the lobby of the CIA’s original headquarters building, this verse is fixed in stone in the old King James wording. The agency’s own history says that Allen Dulles, its fifth and longest-serving director, quoted it at the building’s dedication and insisted that it be set in stone there.

The California Institute of Technology put the same words on its seal: The truth shall make you free. In places like these the truth means knowledge, gathered and tested.

Pope John Paul II pressed the verse in another direction. In his 1993 encyclical Veritatis Splendor he wrote of [[jp2]], and taught that the open acceptance of truth is the condition for real freedom.

Knowledge that frees the mind, moral truth that frees the will: in the passage itself Jesus offers something more personal still, a freedom given by the Son.
point: The truth in this verse is tied to a person and to a condition: remaining in the word of Jesus. The freedom is freedom from sin, and the Son is the one who gives it.
